text: Why are killings immediately after birth overwhelmingly committed by women, while in other filicide cases the gender split becomes much more complicated? In my previous video, I showed that there isn't one universal answer to whether mothers or fathers kill more children. Different countries and datasets give different numbers, but one pattern is particularly consistent. Neonaticide, killing a baby immediately after birth, is overwhelmingly committed by mothers. So why? These cases tend to have a very specific profile. Research commonly finds young women, often unmarried and sometimes in their first pregnancy, who received little or no prenatal care and concealed or denied the pregnancy. Many give birth alone. And interestingly, serious mental illness is actually less common in neonaticides than in many other cases of maternal filicide. Part of the explanation is simply opportunity. In a concealed pregnancy, the mother may literally be the only adult present when the baby is born. The father may not even know the birth is happening or sometimes that there was a pregnancy at all. And the motive is often connected to the pregnancy itself. An unwanted child, fear, shame or fear of how family or others will react. But once we move beyond the immediate newborn period, there isn't one neat explanation anymore. Now we are mixing together several very different kinds of cases. And both mothers and fathers appear in all of them. One pathway is fatal physical abuse. Some research finds fathers and other male caregivers disproportionately represented in abusive head trauma and fatal non-accidental injury. With infants specifically, crying, frustration and loss of control frequently appear in the circumstances leading up to the abuse. But this is absolutely not a male-only phenomenon. A Finnish filicide study actually found mothers dominating death caused by battering, while an England and Wales study found non-accidental injury more common among fathers. Same broad type of crime, different results in different populations. Another important pathway is severe mental illness. This is where the gender difference seems more consistent. In that England and Wales study, 66% of mothers who committed filicide had a history of mental disorder compared with 27% of fathers. Maternal filicide is more often associated in the research with severe depression, psychosis, suicidal thinking and so-called altruistic filicide, where a severely disturbed believes killing the child is somehow protecting or saving them. Fathers can obviously kill while severely mental ill too. But paternal filicide is more often associated with things like physical violence, alcohol or substance misuse, violence towards a partner, jealousy and relationship conflict. And then there's another particularly male-heavy type, familicide, killing a partner and one or more children together. A systematic review found these cases were almost exclusively committed by men. And about half of perpetrators also died by suicide afterwards. And this may be one reason why fathers become increasingly represented as children get older in some datasets. So the answer isn't women do it because they are mentally ill and men do it because they are violent. There's far too much overlap for that. Women commit fatal abuse. Men experience psychosis, depression and suicidal thinking. But the research does point towards some broad differences. Neonaticide is closely connected to concealed or unwanted pregnancy. Maternal filicide is more strongly associated with severe mental illness and suicidal or altruistic motives. Paternal filicide is more strongly associated with physical violence, substance misuse, partner conflict and familicide. And that helps explain why different age groups and different studies can produce such different gender ratios. Filicide isn't really one type of crime with one cause. And reducing all of these very different cases to mothers do it more or fathers do it more lives out probably the most important part of the story.
